t: Range Sum Query 2D - Mutable: From Brute Force to 2D Binary Indexed Tree
o: We must support two operations on a 2D matrix: point updates (set a cell's value) and rectangle sum queries. The classic prefix-sum trick fails here because updating one cell would require rebuilding all prefix sums, costing $O(mn)$ per update. Conversely, brute force answers queries in $O(mn)$ but updates in $O(1)$. With m, n ≤ 200 and at most 5000 calls, even the naive approach passes (5000 × 40000 = 2×10^8 worst case is borderline), so we present it first, then show the optimal 2D Binary Indexed Tree achieving $O(\log m \cdot \log n)$ per operation. In the example, sumRegion(2,1,4,3) sums rows 2–4, cols 1–3 giving 8; after update(3,2,2) changes that cell from 0 to 2, the same query returns 10.
k: Static 2D prefix sums give O(1) queries but O(mn) updates — unusable when updates are interleaved with queries.
A 2D Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick tree) supports both point update and prefix-rectangle sum in O(log m · log n).
To 'set' a cell with a BIT (which supports add), store current values and add val − old value.
Rectangle sums decompose into four 2D prefix sums via inclusion–exclusion: S(r2,c2) − S(r1−1,c2) − S(r2,c1−1) + S(r1−1,c1−1).

a.i: Keep the matrix as-is. Updates write directly to the cell in O(1); each sumRegion iterates over every cell of the requested rectangle and accumulates the total. Given the small constraints (m·n ≤ 40000, ≤ 5000 calls), this fits comfortably within limits.
s: update(row, col, val): set matrix[row][col] = val.
sumRegion: loop r from row1..row2, c from col1..col2, accumulate matrix[r][c].
a.t: O(1) per update, O(mn) per sumRegion — up to ~2×10^8 elementary ops worst case, acceptable for these constraints.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the input matrix.

a.i: Build a Fenwick tree over rows and columns simultaneously: node (i, j) covers the rectangle of cells whose row index falls in (i − lowbit(i), i] and column index in (j − lowbit(j), j]. A point update touches O(log m · log n) nodes by adding lowbit repeatedly; a prefix sum of the rectangle (0,0)..(r,c) is obtained by subtracting lowbits down to zero. Rectangle queries use inclusion–exclusion over four such prefix sums. Since BITs only support addition, we keep a copy of current values and apply delta = val − old on update.
s: Build a (m+1) × (n+1) BIT initialized to zeros; insert each matrix[i][j] via point-add during construction.
Keep a copy `vals` of the matrix to know old values.
update(row, col, val): call internal add(row+1, col+1, val − vals[row][col]) and set vals[row][col] = val.
prefix(r, c): walk i = r while i > 0 subtracting/adding lowbit(i) steps over j similarly, accumulating tree[i][j].
sumRegion: return prefix(row2+1, col2+1) − prefix(row1, col2+1) − prefix(row2+1, col1) + prefix(row1, col1).
a.t: O(mn log m log n) construction (or O(mn) with the linear-build trick), O(log m · log n) per update and per sumRegion (four prefix calls).
a.sp: O(mn) for the BIT and the values copy.

w: In an interview, start with brute force to establish correctness, then propose the 2D BIT as the scalable solution; a segment tree of segment trees or sqrt decomposition also works but is more code. Common pitfalls: forgetting the 1-based indexing shift (+1) required by BITs, using `val` directly instead of the delta `val − old` on update, and messing up inclusion–exclusion signs in sumRegion. Edge cases: single-cell matrices, full-matrix queries (row1=col1=0), negative values (BIT handles them fine since it stores deltas). Likely follow-ups: handle column inserts/deletes (switch to balanced BST / sorted structure), maximize instead of sum (BIT no longer works — need 2D segment tree), or very frequent updates vs. queries trade-offs (sqrt decomposition gives O(√n) both ways).
